newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-CRAZY GANG REWRITE WIMBLEDON LEGEND.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-CRAZY GANG REWRITE WIMBLEDON LEGEND.

text.p: Wimbledon. The word conjures up images of strawberries and cream, ladies in summer frocks, gentlemen in panama hats. Borg and Sampras, King and Graf -- the world's most famous tennis tournament.
At least, those were the associations. Over the last few years, however, it has been flying fists, muddy knees, wincing tackles, shaved heads and bared buttocks. Welcome to Wimbledon F.C.

Once known as the "Crazy Gang" for their heavy drinking and wild ways, Wimbledon are the ugly ducklings who, after only 20 years as a league club, have shocked the establishment again by turning into swans.

Gone are the days of the high, long ball and in their place a more skilful, flowing and attractive game which has won over an army of reluctant admirers. Their league form has dropped off recently but they are still eighth in the premier league and they also reached two Cup semifinals.
In the League Cup, they lost to Leicester on the away goals rule but have another chance for Wembley glory when they play Chelsea at Highbury in the F.A.Cup semifinals on Sunday.
On paper, it should be an easy game to call. Chelsea's side includes names such as Zola, Leboeuf, Di Matteo and Vialli. For Wimbledon, the less cosmopolitan line-up of Earle, Perry, Jones and Gayle.
But it would take a brave man to bet against the team described by one former manager as "the academy of spirit".
The current manager is Joe Kinnear, who made his name as a player with Tottenham Hotspur and won 26 caps for the Republic of Ireland. He is quick to point out the secret of his team's success.

"I've been here six years now and my philosophy remains unchanged. I have a solid base of six home-grown boys who have been with us since kids and all the players I've bought have been hungry," he says.
"What I teach them all is what Bill Nicholson taught me when I was at Spurs. I tell them, 'never give in, never settle for second best and never be in awe of anyone'."

Fighting talk which epitomises the triumph of spirit over adversity. Wimbledon is not a big or rich club in the manner of Manchester United, Arsenal or even Chelsea. Indeed, they do not even have their own ground.

They share Selhurst Park, the home of first division club Crystal Palace, and their home gates are the lowest in the premier league. But, in spite of that, they have always had spirit and hunger for success.
"In our circumstance, Wimbledon should be regarded as the Club of the Century," says club owner and managing director Sam Hammam.
"We are known as the Crazy Gang but, in all honesty, we are the ultimate gladiators. We are not down to any individual but dependent on what we call The Family."
Formed in 1889, Wimbledon won the F.A.Amateur Cup in 1963 but did not join the league until they won the minor Southern League championship in 1977.
Eleven years later, having climbed to the first division in 1986, came the storybook ending when they beat Liverpool 1-0 at Wembley to lift the F.A. Cup.

But if anyone thought that was the end of the upward spiral they were wrong. Within hours of their greatest hour, an experience Hammam described as the "day the club lost its virginity", the team was put up for sale.

Hammam, who bought a majority stake in the club on an impulse because his daughter was born at a Wimbledon hospital, showed his business sense and raised more than 12 million pounds ($19.5 million) from sales in the next six years to secure the club's long-term future.
There are no stars, although recent success has begun to bring international attention.

The captain, Vinnie Jones, the only survivor of the 1988 Cup run, now leads Wales while two players who have come through the youth system, goalkeeper Neil Sullivan and defender Chris Perry, are on the brink of their national teams.
"Wimbledon's success is down to hard work, shrewdness in the transfer market and phenomenal spirit. It's a tribal spirit," says Bobby Gould, who coached them to the F.A. Cup in 1988.
But it also means there is no room for error. Success on the field is imperative if the club are not to fall by the wayside to the premier league's heavyweights.
"The likes of Manchester United, Newcastle and Arsenal have to stay in the top division because of the ego and status symbol," says Hammam.
"We are different. We have to stay up because, if Wimbledon are relegated, we die."
On the evidence of this season, there seems little chance of that.
